texto:
Inventory modes are the three tiers Google uses to decide how much potentially sensitive content an advertiser's YouTube and display ads may appear alongside. Each tier is a single setting, chosen once for an account or advertiser, that trades reach against caution: Maximum admits everything that meets Google's monetisation standards, Moderate removes a band of edgier material, and Limited removes more again. It exists because building exclusions topic by topic proved too fiddly for most buyers and inconsistent across Google's surfaces.
The name is recent. Google Ads still labels the control "inventory type" in much of its interface, while Display & Video 360 (DV360), Google's demand-side platform (DSP), renamed its "content categories" to inventory modes in 2025. Since October 1, 2026, the two have described the same three tiers, and those tiers have become the main suitability lever on Google's buying tools.
How the tiers work
Every tier sits above a fixed floor. Google's Video Ad Safety Promise keeps ads away from content such as profanity in titles or thumbnails, full nudity, drug abuse or sale, and terrorism or sensitive current events whichever tier is selected, according to the Google Ads Help Center. The tiers only govern what happens above that floor.
According to Google's documentation as of October 2026:
- Maximum inventory shows ads across all available inventory that meets monetisation standards. It can include strong profanity in comedy or documentaries, blurred nudity, violence in video games and drug use in music, news or educational content.
- Moderate inventory follows Google's advertiser-friendly guidelines and excludes strong profanity, dramatised violence and sexually suggestive themes. Google describes it as "a good balance between reach and brand suitability".
- Limited inventory also removes moderate profanity and sexually suggestive themes, "even in mainstream content like music videos or makeup tutorials". Google recommends it only for brands with strict requirements and warns that it may limit reach and performance.
Classification happens on Google's side. Machine-learning classifiers and human raters score videos and pages, and each impression opportunity is filtered against the advertiser's tier before the auction. No signal travels in an OpenRTB bid request for this purpose; the decision is internal to Google's owned inventory and its DSP.
Where it is set. In Google Ads, the tier is chosen under Tools, then Content suitability, and applies at account level to Video, Display, Demand Gen and the YouTube and Display portions of Performance Max. It covers in-stream video, Watch Next, Shorts, the Home and Subscription feeds, Google video partners, Display, mobile apps and Discover. It does not apply to Search, Search partners, Gmail, Google Play or App campaigns. In the Google Ads API, the account-level value lives in the customer resource field video_brand_safety_suitability, which uses an enum of the old names: EXPANDED_INVENTORY, STANDARD_INVENTORY and LIMITED_INVENTORY.
In DV360 the mode is set at advertiser level and inherited by every campaign, insertion order and line item; it cannot be edited lower down. Google's DV360 help page states that "all line items use this category by default" in reference to Maximum.
Exceptions. YouTube Sponsorship campaigns, which reserve inventory in advance, run on Moderate even when an account selects Limited. DV360 lets buyers exempt chosen deals on non-reservation display, video, connected TV (CTV) and audio line items from all advertiser-level settings at once, though not YouTube, Demand Gen, Auction Packages or Inventory Packages, and not Google's automatic brand safety protections.
A worked example shows the trade. An advertiser on Maximum may appear on a popular music video with repeated swearing. Moving to Moderate removes that placement but keeps a music video with milder language. Moving to Limited removes both. Since October 2023, Google Ads has shown an "estimated impact" panel comparing inventory, impressions and cost per thousand impressions (CPM) for each tier, according to PPC News Feed.
Origin and evolution
The tiers grew out of the YouTube advertiser crisis of 2017. After The Times reported in February 2017 that ads were running beside extremist videos, brands including Marks & Spencer, HSBC, Audi and L'Oreal pulled UK spending, according to Tubefilter. On March 21, 2017, Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, announced safer default settings and account-level exclusions. In January 2018, Google began manually reviewing Google Preferred channels, its top 5% of YouTube content.
The three-tier inventory type setting arrived in Google Ads in October 2018, replacing a checklist of excludable categories such as tragedy and conflict or profanity, according to Seer Interactive. It ran beside an older system of digital content labels and sensitive category classifiers: 9 classifiers in Google Ads and 16 in DV360 and Campaign Manager.
In October 2022, Google consolidated the controls into a Content Suitability Center covering YouTube and the Display Network. On November 2, 2023, Danielle Wolinsky, Google's global lead for advertiser trust, wrote that Standard was "recommended" for most advertisers and that inventory types had been extended to Shorts.
The redundancy then unwound. From September 2024, digital content labels stopped applying to YouTube line items, except "content suitable for families". In 2025, DV360 renamed "brand safety" to "brand suitability" and "content categories" to "inventory modes", and from June 2025 locked the setting to advertiser level for YouTube and partner line items, according to its help pages. On November 7, 2025, inventory types reached the YouTube Home feed, Watch Next feed and Discover for Video, Demand Gen and Performance Max campaigns.
In April 2026, Google emailed advertisers that Expanded would become Maximum and Standard would become Moderate from May 2026, according to PPC News Feed, with Limited unchanged. The same notice reportedly said accounts that had never chosen a tier would default to Maximum. Screening criteria were not changed.
Why it matters
The mode is now the largest single suitability decision on Google's video and display inventory. Google's June 2026 roadmap warned that "failure to transition brand suitability workflows to the new controls will result in unrestricted serving", and the DV360 API team confirmed on August 27, 2026 that two exclusion targeting types would stop working on October 1. Buyers who relied on those exclusions must now express the same caution through a tier and theme exclusions.
The setting also anchors third-party assurance. YouTube was the first platform accredited by the Media Rating Council (MRC) for content-level brand safety on February 9, 2021, according to Google. On June 3, 2026, that accreditation extended to Shorts and covered all three modes, with a reported advertiser safety error rate below 1% on a 60-day moving average, measured from 2,000 rater-reviewed video samples a day. The MRC itself narrowed what vendors may call "brand safety" in an October 2025 policy.
Limitations and disputes
Google grades its own inventory. The classifiers, the raters and the tier definitions are Google's. Verification firms such as IAS and DoubleVerify measure outcomes after delivery but do not set the tiers, and the MRC scope excludes CTV, live streams, Google video partners and embedded players.
Defaults have loosened. In 2017 Google tightened defaults; by 2026, Performance Max documentation listed Maximum as the default for its YouTube and Display ads. Documentation is inconsistent: as of October 2026, one Google Ads Help page still describes Standard as the default for all accounts while labelling its tables with the new names, and the DV360 help page states Maximum. Both positions are cited here because Google has not reconciled them publicly.
Three tiers are coarse. A beverage brand and a children's toy maker may want different treatment of the same music video, yet both pick from one ladder. Google's own guidance warns that overusing controls raises CPMs and limits reach, and news publishers have long argued that blunt suitability settings defund journalism.
The underlying standard is contested. The tiers echo risk levels from the Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM), which the World Federation of Advertisers discontinued in August 2024 after X sued. On April 15, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and eight states sued WPP, Publicis and Dentsu, alleging a shared brand safety floor restrained competition.
Not the same as
Digital content labels. These were maturity ratings, from DL-G to DL-MA, attached to pages and videos. Advertisers excluded labels one by one. They were retired on YouTube in 2024 and in DV360 programmatic buying on October 1, 2026.
Content theme exclusions. These are topic-level switches, such as Politics, Religion or News (sensitive), applied on top of a mode. DV360 now offers 10. A mode answers "how strict"; a theme answers "which subjects".
Brand suitability. This is the broader discipline, distinct from brand safety, of matching ads to content an individual brand accepts. Inventory modes are one Google implementation of it.
Other platforms' inventory filters. Meta launched Expanded, Moderate and Limited filters for Facebook and Instagram feeds in 2023, mapped to GARM risk levels, and IAS measures how they perform. TikTok introduced Full, Standard and Limited tiers in July 2022, and Amazon DSP opened brand suitability tiers in beta in November 2025. The names overlap; the classifiers do not.
Recent developments
On October 1, 2026, DV360 retired sensitive categories and digital content labels for programmatic display, video, CTV and audio, leaving what Google calls "the 3 core inventory modes (Maximum, Moderate, Limited) and 10 Content themes". As of today, Google's DV360 reference page still described the removed controls. Earlier in 2026, Google removed parked domains from the Search Partner Network on February 10 and gave advertisers a single account-level placement exclusion list across Performance Max, Demand Gen, YouTube and Display. Together these changes leave the mode, a theme list and placement exclusions as the core of suitability on Google inventory.
Timeline
- February 2017: The Times reports ads running beside extremist YouTube videos; major UK brands pause spending.
- March 21, 2017: Philipp Schindler announces safer defaults and account-level exclusions.
- January 2018: Google begins manual review of Google Preferred channels.
- October 2018: Google Ads introduces the Expanded, Standard and Limited inventory type setting.
- February 9, 2021: YouTube receives MRC accreditation for content-level brand safety.
- July 12, 2022: TikTok launches its Inventory Filter with Full, Standard and Limited tiers.
- October 2022: Google launches the Content Suitability Center for YouTube and Display.
- April 2023: Meta launches Expanded, Moderate and Limited inventory filters for feeds.
- October 2023: Google Ads adds an estimated impact comparison for inventory types.
- November 2, 2023: Google confirms inventory types extended to YouTube Shorts.
- August 2024: The WFA discontinues GARM.
- September 2024: Digital content labels stop applying to YouTube ads.
- 2025: DV360 renames content categories to inventory modes.
- June 2025: DV360 locks YouTube content category settings to advertiser level.
- November 7, 2025: Inventory types extend to YouTube Home feed, Watch Next feed and Discover.
- April 2026: Google announces Expanded becomes Maximum and Standard becomes Moderate from May 2026.
- April 15, 2026: FTC and eight states sue WPP, Publicis and Dentsu over brand safety standards.
- June 3, 2026: MRC accreditation extends to YouTube Shorts across all three modes.
- August 27, 2026: DV360 API team confirms removal of two exclusion targeting types.
- October 1, 2026: DV360 consolidates suitability into three inventory modes and 10 content themes.

Summary
Who: Google operates inventory modes in Google Ads and Display & Video 360. Advertisers and agencies choose a tier; Google's classifiers and human raters apply it; the MRC audits the YouTube system, and verification firms measure results.
What: A three-tier brand suitability setting, Maximum, Moderate and Limited, that sets how much sensitive content ads may appear beside, above a fixed floor of excluded content.
When: The tiers launched in Google Ads in October 2018 as Expanded, Standard and Limited. DV360 adopted the "inventory modes" name in 2025, Google Ads renamed two tiers in May 2026, and DV360 made the modes its core control on October 1, 2026.
Where: YouTube in-stream, Shorts, feeds and Watch Next, Google video partners, the Google Display Network, Discover and, in DV360, programmatic display, video, CTV and audio. Search, Gmail, Google Play and App campaigns are not covered.
Why: The setting was created after the 2017 YouTube advertiser crisis to give buyers a simple way to balance reach against caution, and has since absorbed older label and category controls that Google retired.
